Modern.brandNameRationale: Two words. New Pour says what's in the glass and the brand's posture at the same time. The brand sits on the act of opening something modern, the bottle that wasn't on the list last year.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern wine retail has been moving toward natural wine, low-intervention producers, and design-led shop fronts. Customers are design-literate, slightly burnt out on long origin stories, and looking for shops that respect their time.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Discovery Wines (discoverywines.com) holds the modern shop position. Henry & Son (henryandson.co) sits in the design-led tier. Verve Wine (vervewine.com) does the editorial-led middle. Wine.com (wine.com) is the mass-market giant. We sit closer to Henry & Son in posture.
Modern.positioningStatement: A modern wine shop that picks the bottle so you don't have to read four paragraphs first.

targetAudience.primary: 28 to 45. Buys wine weekly. Already follows two natural wine accounts. Wants the shop to filter the noise. Will pay a premium for editorial taste.

dos: Show the producer, the region, the price
Write tasting notes in plain English
Recommend three bottles per dinner
donts: Use the word terroir without explaining it
Write tasting notes that say 'forest floor'

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. NEW POUR in a tight modern grotesk, all caps, two words on one line. A small geometric mark, a single tilted rectangle suggesting a wine glass viewed from the side, used as the favicon and on the shipping carton seal.

colorPalette.name: Pour Red
colorPalette.meaning: The single accent. The color of a young red.

typography.secondary: GT America Mono for vintages and prices
typography.rationale: One family. The mono carries the vintage and the price. The regular carries the brand and the editorial copy.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A site that loads the weekly recommendation first. A small shop with a printed list reprinted weekly. A monthly newsletter with three bottles and what to cook with them. No app.

Modern.tagline: Wines from the edge of the appellation.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Verge is a real word for the edge of something — the road, the field, the season. It points to where the grapes are grown (the boundary between two soils, two climates, two appellations) without naming the place. Wine Co. is the plain category suffix. Reads in the lineage of modern wine brands like Day Wines, Broc Cellars, Field Recordings — evocative but never literal.
Modern.manifesto: Most modern wine brands sell either a place or a varietal. We made Verge because the actual interesting wines are made on the boundaries — the cold side of the hill, the last picking before the rain, the parcel that nobody planted on purpose. The brand is the edge, not the center. Each bottle is from a single parcel we lease at the verge of something larger.
Modern.industrySummary: DTC wine has matured around two camps: the heritage estate (Caymus, Silver Oak) and the natural-wine bottle-shop set (Maison Noir, Broc). The opening underneath is for a modern grower-producer brand that talks about specific parcels in plain language, ships direct, and looks more like a design studio than a cellar.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Day Wines (daywines.com) holds the modern grower-producer slot well. Broc Cellars (broccellars.com) plays the natural-wine peer. Field Recordings (fieldrecordingswine.com) sits in the editorial-modern middle. Caymus (caymus.com) is the heritage reference we are not. We sit closer to Day and Field Recordings, with a single-parcel framing per bottle.
Modern.positioningStatement: Verge Wine Co. is a modern grower-producer that releases small-lot wines from single parcels on the edge of their appellations.
Modern.positioningRationale: We compete on specificity. Each label names the parcel, the elevation, the soil, the year. The customer is buying a specific patch of ground in a specific year — not a brand and not a varietal.

targetAudience.primary: Wine buyers 30–50 who have moved past supermarket bottles but are not chasing collector wines.
behaviors: Talk about a wine by parcel, not by score.
motivations: Want to drink wines they can talk about.
Want to know where the grapes come from.
Want to support producers, not distributors.

Write back labels like a short field note.

messagingPillars.name: One parcel per bottle

messagingPillars.name: The edge
messagingPillars.description: We seek parcels on the boundary of an appellation, on a transitional soil, or at the limit of a varietal's comfortable climate. The interesting wine is at the edge.

messagingPillars.name: Direct only

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark — Verge set in a calm modern grotesque with a small horizontal rule beneath, almost like a topographic line. The mark sits on the label small; the parcel name is the largest type on the front.

colorPalette.name: Slate

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two names with French rhythm. Petit suggests smallness and care. Côte is the wine term for a slope (Côte d'Or, Côte Rôtie). The pair reads as a small heritage merchant with a quiet cellar of important bottles.
Luxury.story: Petit & Côte was founded by two principals who had spent decades inside larger fine wine houses and wanted to keep a smaller cellar. The firm represents a limited number of producers. Some clients have been buying through the firm since it opened.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end fine wine has been moving toward larger auction houses and faster transactions. There's a parallel market for small merchants with deep relationships, both with producers and with collectors. The customer is paying for the merchant's eye, not the catalog.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Berry Bros. & Rudd (bbr.com) holds the institutional London reference. Acker Merrall & Condit (ackerwines.com) sits in the auction-meets-merchant tier. Skurnik Wines (skurnikwines.com) does the importer-led version in the US. We sit smaller and quieter than all of them.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small fine wine merchant with a private list and a long client book.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy. Often inherited. Builds a cellar over decades. Trusts a small number of merchants by name. Values the relationship with the principal.

dos: Address the client by surname
Name the producer, the vineyard, the vintage
Send paper allocations by post

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark with elegant ligatures. A small hand-drawn ampersand becomes the firm's hallmark, used on labels, the printed allocation cards, and the wax seal of every paper letter.

colorPalette.name: Cellar Burgundy

Luxury.brandNameRationale: A plausible French château name in the heritage-estate convention. Aurigny is a real but small Channel Islands place-name that reads as Old World without being a famous appellation. The 'Château d'X' format places the brand in the Bordeaux/Loire tradition without imitating any specific producer.
Luxury.story: Château d'Aurigny is a single-estate winery on twenty-three hectares, in continuous family ownership since 1873. Production is held to two cuvées — a single red and a single white — released each spring. The cellar master has been at the estate for thirty-one years.
Luxury.industrySummary: Premium Old-World wine has consolidated into well-known appellations and négociant houses. There is a quieter market for the small single-estate producer in continuous family ownership — twenty to fifty hectares, deliberately small catalog, multi-generational cellar staff.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Domaine de la Romanée-Conti (romanee-conti.fr) is the unreachable reference. Domaine Leroy (domaineleroy.com) is the peer in restraint. Vega Sicilia (vega-sicilia.com) sits in the iconic single-estate slot. We belong with single-estate, multi-generational producers — narrower in catalog than any of them.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A single-estate Old World winery producing two cuvées per year, family-owned since 1873.
Luxury.positioningRationale: We do not extend the catalog. The estate is the limit. The two cuvées have remained the same for four generations.

behaviors: Hold mixed cases of single producers across vintages.

Want continuity of cellar staff and style.
Want allocations they can rely on.

Reference vintages by year and weather.

messagingPillars.description: One red, one white. The composition is published. We have not added a third in four generations and we will not.

messagingPillars.name: The cellar master

messagingPillars.name: Allocation by mailing list

typography.secondary: An engraver's italic for vintage years and signatures.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word. Glass is the unit of wine drinking. The brand sits on the object, not the bottle, not the vintage, not the maker. Plain, honest, and slightly disarming.
Minimal.industrySummary: Wine brands have elaborate names and longer stories. There's an opening for one that strips it back to the smallest object in the experience.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most wine brands fail this purity test. The closest peer in spirit is some Japanese sake brands and the no-name aesthetic of Muji's table wine line, if it existed.
Minimal.positioningStatement: A small wine list of bottles meant to be poured by the glass.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who order wine by the glass and don't want to read a wine list. They want one to three good options at known prices.

dos: Show the wine, the price by the glass
Confirm orders in one line
Use plain English

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. GLASS in a single weight grotesk, wide kerned, all caps, five letters with generous space. No icon. The bar menu, the bottle shop label, and the receipt all carry the wordmark and nothing else.

Minimal.tagline: One parcel. One wine. One year.
Minimal.brandNameRationale: Plot Eleven names the eleventh parcel on a single vineyard map. The naming convention belongs to grower-producers like Hill Farmstead's 'Civil Disobedience' series or Burgundy's lieu-dit tradition — the parcel is the brand. Reads as honest, almost industrial, with no marketing wrapper.
Minimal.manifesto: Wine branding has buried what the bottle is. We made Plot Eleven because the bottle is a single parcel, in a single year, made into a single wine. The label is the plot number, the year, and the variety. The marketing is the wine.
Minimal.industrySummary: Single-vineyard, single-parcel labeling is well-established in Burgundy and increasingly in the New World. There is room for a minimal brand that takes the parcel-as-brand premise all the way — no estate name, no producer name above the parcel, no marketing copy.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Burlotto (burlotto.com) plays in the single-parcel Italian space. Tyler Winery (tylerwinery.com) holds the minimal-parcel-led American slot. Maison Noir is a peer in restraint. We sit further out — the parcel number is the brand.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Plot Eleven is a single-parcel wine project releasing one wine per year from one vineyard parcel.
Minimal.positioningRationale: We strip the label to the parcel number, the year, and the variety. The producer is named in small type on the back. The parcel does the work.

Corporate.tagline: Wine distribution and import at scale.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Three words. Vineyard signals the source. Holdings Group names the corporate structure. The whole name reads like a real, established wine importer and distributor already on the panel at major retailers and restaurant groups.
Corporate.industrySummary: Wine importing and distribution is a serious B2B category dominated by major importers (Southern Glazer's, RNDC, Breakthru) and a few specialist firms. The buyers are retail chains, restaurant groups, and on-premise operators. Brand and operational discipline are the differentiators.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Southern Glazer's Wine & Spirits (southernglazers.com) holds the giant peer position. RNDC (rndc-usa.com) sits at the same tier. Skurnik Wines (skurnikwines.com) does the design-led import middle. We sit smaller, focused on the contemporary fine wine and natural wine middle market.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Wine importing and distribution for fine wine retailers and restaurant groups at scale.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Retailers and restaurant groups want partners who can deliver consistent fine wine and natural wine supply at scale. The category incumbents are designed for legacy distribution. We are designed for the contemporary buyer.

Corporate.tagline: Vineyard ownership and wine production at scale.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Heaton is a Yorkshire-origin surname with an agricultural register. Vail is a short, hard-edged surname pulled from the German Veil, meaning vellum. Together the surnames read as an established vineyard partnership operating multiple estates — the kind of holding entity that supplies bulk programs and retail private label, not consumer-facing premium.
Corporate.manifesto: Heaton & Vail Vineyards is a vineyard ownership and wine production company operating across multiple AVAs and appellations. We grow grapes on owned and leased land, produce wine under contract for retail private label and restaurant programs, and operate two regional bottling facilities. The buyer is a retail wine buyer, a hospitality group, or a private-label client.
Corporate.industrySummary: Mid-tier wine production is consolidating under a small number of large operators with multi-estate footprints. The opening is for a serious vineyard-and-production company with operational depth, transparent pricing, and the capacity to handle private-label and contract production for retailers and hospitality groups.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Constellation Brands (cbrands.com) is the global reference. Treasury Wine Estates (tweglobal.com) holds the multi-estate peer slot. Trinchero Family Estates (tfewines.com) sits in the family-owned mid-tier middle. We belong in the regional multi-estate operator category.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Heaton & Vail Vineyards is a multi-AVA vineyard ownership and wine production company serving retail private label and hospitality contract production.
Corporate.positioningRationale: We compete on production capacity, AVA breadth, and the consistency required by retail and hospitality buyers. The product is reliable wine at agreed specifications, year after year.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Two words. Second Bottle is the moment a dinner gets good. The brand names the threshold of a real conversation. Loud, warm, and slightly cheeky.
Creative.manifesto: Most wine brands sell the first sip. The reverent moment. The notes on the back of the label. We made Second Bottle because the truth about wine is that the second one is when things get interesting. The brand is for the dinner that runs long, the conversation that gets honest, the moment people stop pretending to know what tannin means.
Creative.industrySummary: Wine branding has been earnest, terroir-led, and slightly precious. There's room for a brand that's loud, character-driven, sticker-friendly, and serious about good wine without taking itself too seriously.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Black Lips Brewing isn't wine but does this voice. Big Bad Wines (bigbadwines.com) sits closer. Some Young Punks (someyoungpunks.com) holds the irreverent label position. We sit warmer and more retail-friendly than any of them.
Creative.positioningStatement: A wine brand for the dinner that runs long.

Creative.tagline: Wines that don't take themselves seriously.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Marigold is a real botanical name, warm and slightly sun-faded — the opposite of the somber heritage register most wine brands use. 'Wine Project' frames the brand as ongoing and experimental rather than canonical. The pairing belongs to the contemporary creative wine school (Field Recordings, Day Wines, Broc Cellars) without copying any of them.
Creative.manifesto: Most wine brands are trying to sound like a 17th-century estate even when the winemaker is 34 and learned in a garage. We started Marigold because the actual fun of making wine right now is unfussy — co-fermenting weird varieties, releasing pet-nats with cartoon labels, putting a sticker on a bottle and seeing what happens. The brand is a project. The labels change. The wine is honest about being made by humans in a warehouse last September.
Creative.industrySummary: Natural and low-intervention wine has matured into a fully developed market with its own canon. There is real space for a brand that takes the creative-led wine premise and pushes harder on illustration, voice, and label design — closer to a record label than a winery.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Broc Cellars (broccellars.com) is the closest creative peer. Maison Noir (mnwines.com) holds the irreverent slot. Field Recordings (fieldrecordingswine.com) sits in the editorial-creative middle. Las Jaras (lasjaras.com) plays in the celebrity-creative position. We sit alongside Broc and Maison Noir, with a slightly louder visual register.
Creative.positioningStatement: Marigold Wine Project is a creative-led wine label releasing small-lot experimental wines with illustrated labels and an irreverent voice.
Creative.positioningRationale: The brand competes on personality and design as much as on the wine itself. Each release has its own commissioned label illustration. The brand voice is closer to a fanzine than a tasting room.

typography.secondary: A neutral grotesque for body and field data.
